title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to evaluate whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) used gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the primary checker. Execution (2026‑08‑30T11:50:34 → 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07 UTC) processed 200 tasks with a single shared initial generation per task (model_calls_used = 200), allowed up to 200 repair calls but applied none because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected failure rate was 0% on this curated task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully tested. We report the sealed design, deterministic accounting, representative diagnostics, contamination‑check evidence (Mininet 10% holdout → 20 tasks; zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Prior proposals therefore combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR). The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by a fixed generator/prompt policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We ask a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions are: (1) a sealed paired preregistered design (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate the marginal effect of validator+repair; (2) a fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded null/degenerate outcome analysis that clarifies when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures and what operational measurements practitioners should collect prior to deploying GVR.
sections.related_work: LLMs exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity across domains; mitigation approaches include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded agent architectures. Prior NetOps prototypes show feasibility for intent→configuration generation but typically lack instrumented production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops are proposed to improve safety; complementary red‑team work documents configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can change safety outcomes. Surveys and prototype evaluations motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals by measuring a prespecified paired estimand under archived, deterministic conditions and by reporting contamination checks via an emulator holdout.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The experiment was preregistered (study_id = cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02; preregistration SHA‑256 a9e5d64c...) with a paired design (n = 200 tasks), a single primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and an adapter‑enforced maximum model‑call cap (400). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; 95% CIs used a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks covering four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states and explicit workflow constraints (for example: make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields). The primary deterministic checker deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces these task‑encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). As preregistered, a Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator served as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to flag validator–emulator mismatches; the execution produced a contamination_summary.csv reporting zero disagreements.

Model, adapter, and shared‑initial semantics. The run used the declared hosted model gpt‑5‑mini invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single deterministic initial candidate (one model call per task) which was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This precluded per‑condition re‑sampling variance and isolates the purely validator/repair influence on an identical generator output. The adapter accounting records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}.

Repair policy and handling rules. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task when the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed in principle but only triggered if validation failed. Exclusion and missingness rules were fixed: pairs where neither condition completed due to infrastructure failures would be excluded; tasks flagged for validator–emulator disagreement were predeclared to be excluded from the primary analysis and reported in sensitivity analyses. All decisions and logs were archived deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and descriptive outcomes. The autonomous run executed from 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059+00:00 to 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650+00:00 and completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Analysis artifacts show baseline_successes = 200/200 and guarded_successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity, contamination checks, and reconciliation. Because no initial candidate failed validation, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm pair_accounting_consistent = true and all deterministic consistency checks passed. Provider accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200, consistent with single shared initial calls per task reused deterministically across conditions.

Representative diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched the task required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0. Difficulty annotations in validator traces (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) demonstrate that tasks exercised nontrivial workflow constraints (medium→very_hard) despite producing validator‑satisfying candidates. These examples substantiate that the task bank contained constrained, realistic patterns yet the chosen generator+prompting policy produced correct outputs for this curated set.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates an important practical point: when a chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step has no validator‑detectable failures to reduce. This does not imply GVR is never useful; rather, GVR’s marginal operational benefit is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage and fidelity.

Why baseline failures were zero (artifact‑grounded). The archive supports multiple, non‑exclusive explanations: (1) the prompt template and shared_initial semantics produced candidates that conform closely to explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes required_sequences that map directly to deterministic validator checks and are therefore comparatively easier to satisfy with a deterministic generation policy; (3) the primary validator enforces the task‑encoded constraints but may omit certain end‑to‑end device idiosyncrasies visible only under full device emulation or production execution; and (4) the shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a mechanism that might have produced alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational implications and recommendations. Before investing in automated repair automation, practitioners should (a) measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workload distributions; (b) assess validator coverage via emulation or staged device tests (the preregistered Mininet holdout is an example); (c) consider richer generator strategies (multi‑sample, multi‑model) to produce repairable candidates when needed; and (d) prioritize validator fidelity (vendor/device semantics) if baseline failure rates are low. When baseline failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains will depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness.

Reproducibility note and known gap. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters) are archived. The contamination summary documents the Mininet holdout execution and reports zero disagreements for the 10% randomized sample (20 tasks). A known reproducibility gap remains: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive, which prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout despite the contamination summary evidence of zero disagreements. We disclose this gap and provide the contamination summary as evidence that emulator checks were executed and yielded no flags.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules protect against post‑hoc design changes, but the shared_initial design trades generality for experimental control by eliminating per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator enforces task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level behaviors; secondary emulation reduces that risk but cannot fully replicate heterogenous production devices. External validity: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), single sampling policy, and curated task bank limit generalizability to other models, sampling temperatures, adversarial distributions, or operational environments. Conclusion validity: the planned McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nonetheless reporting the observed zero‑discordance outcome is an operational datum that informs future workload selection and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs); no repair attempts were invoked. The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable because the baseline failure rate was 0% on this curated bank. This outcome emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulation or real‑device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for inspection.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
